section.title: Average rate of change
section.p: A limit of average rates cannot be understood until the average rate itself is clear. So we begin with the ordinary slope between two points.
If f is a function and the input changes from a to b, then the output changes from f(a) to f(b). The average rate of change compares these two changes:
This is the slope of the line through the two graph points
That line is called a secant line.

exercise.title: Why is an average rate a secant slope rather than a local slope?

statement.p: The average rate of change of f from a to b is the slope of the line through (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)). In your own words, why does that number describe the whole interval at once, and why is it not the slope of the graph at every point in between?

hint.p: A secant uses two points. On a curved graph, nearby pairs of points can produce different slopes.

paragraphs.title: Displacement, not distance traveled
paragraphs.p: Average velocity uses signed change in position:
If an object moves forward and then backward, its displacement can be small even if it traveled a long distance.
For example, suppose a runner starts at 0 meters, runs to 100 meters, and then returns to 0 meters in 20 seconds. The average velocity over the full trip is
That does not mean the runner was standing still. It means the net change in position was 0. Average velocity measures net signed change per unit time.

exercise.title: Why can average velocity be zero even if the object moved?

statement.p: A runner who goes out and back in 20 seconds has average velocity 0. In your own words, why does that not mean the runner stood still, and what quantity is average velocity actually using?

hint.p: Average velocity uses signed change in position. Distance traveled counts every step, forward or back.

The coffee cools more slowly later. The average rate depends on the interval.

figure.caption: Average rates from data are secant slopes between measured points.

subsection.p: A table gives only certain points. We can compute average rates between those points, but we cannot know the exact instantaneous rate from the table alone. We can estimate it by using nearby data, but the estimate depends on the quality and spacing of the measurements.

exercise.title: Why does reversing the endpoints leave the secant slope unchanged?

statement.p: Computing from b back to a changes the sign of both the numerator and the denominator. In your own words, why is the average rate the same either way, and what geometric object is being measured?

hint.p: A line through two points has one slope. Changing the order of the two points does not change the line.

note.title: Meaning before formulas
note.p: An average rate of change is always a comparison:
note.md: \frac{\text{how much the output changed}}{\text{how much the input changed}}.
note.p: The units tell what kind of comparison it is.

subsection.p: Average rates are useful, but they still describe an interval. A speedometer does not report the average velocity over the last hour. It reports what is happening now.
To get that number from position, we must make the interval shrink.

exercise.title: Why do units and the chosen interval both matter?

statement.p: An average rate always has the form output units per input unit, and its value depends on which two data points we compare. In your own words, why do the units tell the meaning of the comparison, and why can a table give average rates without giving an exact instantaneous rate?

hint.p: A quotient inherits units from numerator and denominator. A table only supplies certain points, so any rate computed from it still belongs to an interval.
